Selene

A Van Gogh Experience in Light & Philosophy

Today's Reflection

Theme: Van Gogh's Philosophy · Mood: serene

Van Gogh painted over 30 self-portraits, not out of vanity but out of necessity — he could not afford models. In each one, the gaze is searching, as if he were trying to paint not his face but his soul.

— Art History

“I often think that the night is more alive and more richly colored than the day. — Vincent van Gogh”

The Moon & Selene

In the beginning, there was darkness — and then Selene rose. The ancient Greeks saw her as a silver chariot crossing the night, but she was more than a goddess. She was the first mirror, the original reflector of light, the celestial body that taught humanity that one can shine without being the source.

Selene, the Greek Titaness of the Moon, drove her silver chariot across the night sky, illuminating the world with borrowed light — a reminder that even reflection can be a form of brilliance.

— Greek Mythology

The Moon controls the tides of the ocean and the tides of the mind. In Vedic thought, Chandra governs the Manas — the emotional mind — and its phases mirror the cycles of human desire and detachment.

— Vedic Astrology

Selene fell in love with the mortal Endymion, asking Zeus to grant him eternal sleep so he would never fade. The Moon's love is possessive — it wants to freeze beauty in time, yet beauty exists only because it passes.

— Greek Mythology

“The Moon is a friend for the lonesome to talk to. — Carl Sandburg”

Ego, Arrogance & The Waves

The wave does not know it is the ocean. It rises, believes itself unique, crashes against the shore, and dissolves — only to rise again. This is the cycle of ego: the endless assertion of separateness, the desperate claim of individuality against the vast indifference of the sea.

The Bhagavad Gita warns: 'The ego is the greatest enemy of the human soul.' When Arjuna asks Krishna about the nature of the self, the answer is not 'I am great' but 'I am not the doer.'

— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 3

Arrogance is the ego's armor. But armor is heavy — it slows the warrior. The Gita teaches that true strength comes not from the assertion of self but from the surrender to dharma.

— Philosophical Reflection

In the ocean of existence, arrogance is a wave that believes it is separate from the sea. It rises, it crashes, and it returns — never having been anything but water.

— Vedantic Philosophy

“The ego is not master in its own house. — Sigmund Freud”

The Bhagavad Gita

On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, between two armies of cousins, a conversation took place that would echo through millennia. Arjuna, paralyzed by doubt, and Krishna, the charioteer who was also God — their dialogue is not about war. It is about the war within.

The Bhagavad Gita begins not with wisdom but with despair. Arjuna, the greatest warrior, drops his bow and says, 'I will not fight.' The scripture teaches that the darkest moment precedes the greatest clarity.

— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 1

Krishna's central teaching: 'You have the right to work, but never to the fruit of work.' This is not passivity — it is the ultimate freedom. Act fully, attach to nothing.

— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 2, Verse 47

The Gita describes the soul as 'unborn, eternal, ever-existing, undying, and primeval.' It is not slain when the body is slain. This is not metaphor — it is the foundational axiom of Hindu philosophy.

— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 2, Verse 20

In Chapter 11, Krishna reveals his Vishvarupa — the Universal Form — containing all worlds, all beings, all time. Arjuna sees the entirety of existence in one being and trembles. The infinite is not abstract; it is terrifyingly real.

— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 11

“The soul is neither born, and nor does it die. — Bhagavad Gita 2.20”

The Shiv Purana

Before there was creation, there was Shiva — not as a being, but as a possibility. The Shiv Purana does not begin with ‘In the beginning’ but with ‘In the endless.’ Shiva is the stillness that contains all motion, the silence that holds all music, the void that is not empty but infinitely full.

In the Shiv Purana, Shiva is described as Nirguna — without attributes, without form, without beginning or end. He is not a god among gods but the ground of being itself, the silence between notes.

— Shiv Purana, Vidyeshwara Samhita

The Shiv Purana teaches that the universe is Shiva's dance — the Tandava. Every atom moves in rhythm. Destruction is not the opposite of creation; it is its partner in an eternal dance.

— Shiv Purana, Rudra Samhita

Shiva drank the poison Halahala to save the universe, turning his throat blue. The Neelakantha — the blue-throated one — teaches that the willingness to suffer for others is the highest form of divinity.

— Shiv Purana, Samudra Manthan

The Shiv Purana describes the damaru — Shiva's drum — as the source of all language and music. The first sound, Nada, is the vibration from which all creation emerges. Music is not entertainment; it is cosmology.

— Shiv Purana

“I am the death that carries off all things, and the source of things to come. — Shiva, Bhagavad Gita 10.34”

Van Gogh’s Vision

Vincent van Gogh did not paint what he saw. He painted what he felt. His stars are not points of light but swirling vortices of energy. His sunflowers are not botanical studies but meditations on mortality. His cypresses are not trees but flames reaching toward heaven.

Van Gogh wrote: 'I dream of painting and then I paint my dream.' For him, art was not representation but revelation — the act of making visible what the eye cannot see.

— Vincent van Gogh, Letters to Theo

The sunflowers Van Gogh painted were not decorative. They were a meditation on life and death — some blooms fresh and golden, others wilting and brown. He painted the full cycle in a single canvas.

— Art Analysis

Van Gogh's 'Starry Night' was painted from memory during the day, at the Saint-Paul-de-Muse asylum. The night he painted was not the night he saw — it was the night he felt.

— Art History

“I often think that the night is more alive and more richly colored than the day. — Vincent van Gogh”
